name: William Jennings Bryan
role: American Democratic politician (1860-1925): congressman, three-time presidential nominee, Secretary of State, Scopes trial prosecutor
summary: Bryan, Nebraska congressman and Democratic presidential nominee in 1896, 1900 and 1908, championed free silver, the income tax and farmers and labor against the gold standard and the banks, and voted for tariff reduction in the House.

sources.title: Voteview roll calls of William Jennings Bryan (ICPSR 1179), US House 1891-1895
sources.author: Voteview, UCLA (Lewis et al.)
sources.usedFor: House votes in the 52nd and 53rd Congresses: Chinese exclusion bill HR6185 (4 April and 4 May 1892, YEA); Sherman silver-purchase repeal HR1 (28 Aug 1893: YEA on amendments for silver bullion certificates #6 and for silver purchases #11, NAY on final passage #12, 239-109); Wilson tariff-reduction bill HR4864 (1 Feb 1894, passage #99 YEA, 204-140).

sources.title: 'Cross of Gold' speech, Democratic National Convention, Chicago, 9 July 1896 (text, Nebraska State Historical Society / Nebraska Studies PDF)
sources.author: William Jennings Bryan
sources.usedFor: Money as a function of government, the income tax, farmers and wage earners as business men, labour against the gold standard.

notes: First audit. Evidence is his House roll calls in the 52nd and 53rd Congresses (Voteview; the keyword scan covered silver, tariff, Chinese, income tax, bank, pension, railroad) the Cross of Gold speech, and two Gutenberg books (In His Image, 1922; The Old World and Its Ways, 1907, read by theme: Philippines, Chinese exclusion, municipal ownership, suffrage, trusts; In His Image on evolution, religion, war and liquor). The 1915 resignation letter (Gutenberg 26377, Current History) was read: he resigned over the second Lusitania note 'to promote the prevention of war', which maps to no statement. His 1914 suffrage handbill, 1900 Imperialism address and In His Image's 'Origin of Man' passages on schools were added in a second pass; prohibition (the Eighteenth Amendment is praised in In His Image) and cooling-off treaties have no matching statement or open text. In The Old World he also noted the Swiss initiative and referendum and Swedish labour laws, which map to no statement. His presidential campaigns, Scopes-era views (creationism, Prohibition) and Secretary of State record are not covered because no open full text was reached, so those statements stay null. The Stanford Record corpus holds no House speeches by him.
